questions.question: Design a product for elderly people.

sampleAnswer.overview: I'd use the CIRCLES framework to structure my answer.

steps.Comprehend: What type of product — hardware, software, or service? Let's focus on a mobile app to help elderly people live independently.
steps.Identify: Primary users: adults 65+, many with limited tech experience, possible vision/motor impairments. Secondary: adult children who want to monitor parents.
steps.Report needs: Stay connected with family, manage medications, access emergency help quickly, combat loneliness.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Most critical: safety and emergency access. Biggest pain point: current apps are too complex for elderly users.
steps.List solutions: 1) One-tap emergency SOS with GPS. 2) Simplified medication reminder with large UI. 3) Family video check-in. 4) Voice-first interface.
steps.Evaluate: SOS + medication reminder has highest impact/effort ratio. Voice-first reduces barrier to entry. Family check-in builds habit loop.
steps.Summarize: Build a voice-first companion app with large-text UI, daily medication reminders, and one-tap SOS. Launch MVP with SOS + reminders, then add family check-in.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Clarifies scope, identifies 2+ user segments, prioritizes needs, proposes 3+ solutions with clear tradeoffs, recommends one with reasoning
evaluationRubric.good: Uses CIRCLES partially, identifies main user, proposes multiple solutions
evaluationRubric.fair: Some structure but jumps to solution, limited user empathy
evaluationRubric.poor: No framework, single solution, no user consideration

keyPoints: Simple UI with large touch targets

questions.question: Design a product for drivers in rush hour.

sampleAnswer.overview: Using CIRCLES to design a rush-hour driver product.

steps.Comprehend: Scope: mobile app for commuters, not commercial drivers. Rush hour = 7-9am and 5-7pm.
steps.Identify: Daily commuters 25-50, stressed, time-constrained, may be carpooling.
steps.Report needs: Reduce commute time, reduce stress, stay informed about delays, use commute productively.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest pain: unpredictable delays. Most underserved: productive use of stuck time.
steps.List solutions: 1) Hyper-accurate predictive routing with ML. 2) Commute podcast/audio content tied to route length. 3) Carpool matching. 4) Real-time parking availability.
steps.Evaluate: Predictive routing improves core need. Audio content is differentiator vs. Waze. Carpool has network effects.
steps.Summarize: AI routing + commute-length audio content as MVP. Carpool as phase 2.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Distinguishes commuter vs. commercial, surfaces stress/time pain points, creative differentiated solution
evaluationRubric.fair: Mentions routing but doesn't go beyond Waze-clone thinking
evaluationRubric.poor: No user research, just lists features

questions.question: How would you improve Facebook Groups?

sampleAnswer.overview: I'd start by clarifying the goal — engagement, retention, or new user acquisition — then use CIRCLES.

steps.Comprehend: Goal: increase meaningful engagement in Groups. Platform: mobile-first.
steps.Identify: Power users (community admins), casual lurkers, new members, local community users.
steps.Report needs: Admins: easier moderation. Lurkers: relevant content without noise. New members: onboarding. Local users: hyper-local discovery.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest drop-off: new members who join but never post. Biggest opportunity: turning lurkers into contributors.
steps.List solutions: 1) AI-suggested first post for new members. 2) Topic threads within groups. 3) Group health score for admins. 4) Local group discovery map.
steps.Evaluate: AI first-post reduces barrier; thread organization reduces noise. Admin health score enables better moderation at scale.
steps.Summarize: Launch topic threads + AI-assisted first post. Measure: post rate of new members in 30 days.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Clarifies business goal, segments users well, proposes measurable improvements with success metrics
evaluationRubric.good: Multiple user types, concrete features, some metrics

keyPoints: Admin vs. lurker vs. new member
Success metric: post rate in 30 days

questions.question: Design a product to help people find parking.

sampleAnswer.overview: Using CIRCLES for a parking product.

steps.Comprehend: Urban parking discovery and reservation, mobile-first.
steps.Identify: Daily urban commuters, event attendees, delivery drivers, handicapped drivers.
steps.Report needs: Find available spots quickly, know price upfront, avoid circling blocks, accessible spots.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Highest frustration: not knowing availability in advance. Most revenue opportunity: reservation.
steps.List solutions: 1) Real-time availability map with IoT sensors. 2) Advance reservation + payment. 3) Dynamic pricing. 4) Accessible spot filter.
steps.Evaluate: Real-time map needs sensor partnerships (high effort). Reservation is highest monetization. Accessible filter is low effort, high goodwill.
steps.Summarize: Partner with garages for reservation API first. Add IoT sensor data in phase 2. Launch accessible filter at launch.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Addresses supply-side partnership challenge, dynamic pricing insight, accessible user segment
evaluationRubric.fair: App idea but ignores supply constraints

questions.question: Design the next version of Apple Watch.

sampleAnswer.overview: Clarify: new hardware iteration or new software capabilities? I'll focus on new software capabilities for Watch OS.

steps.Comprehend: Enhance Apple Watch for health-focused users. Assume same hardware, new software.
steps.Identify: Fitness enthusiasts, chronic condition patients (diabetes, heart), elderly, productivity users.
steps.Report needs: More actionable health insights, earlier warning of health issues, seamless integration with care providers.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest unmet need: translating health data into action. Current gap: data without context.
steps.List solutions: 1) AI health coaching with daily nudges. 2) Doctor-share health report PDF. 3) Medication adherence tracking. 4) Fall prediction (pre-fall vs. post-fall detection).
steps.Evaluate: AI coaching has broad appeal. Doctor-share enables care coordination. Fall prediction is breakthrough for elderly segment.
steps.Summarize: AI health coach + doctor-share report as flagship features for Watch OS next release.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Distinguishes hardware vs. software scope, addresses health ecosystem integration, care provider as stakeholder
evaluationRubric.good: Health focus with multiple user segments

questions.question: Design a product for frequent business travelers.

sampleAnswer.overview: CIRCLES applied to business travel product.

steps.Comprehend: B2B-leaning product for road warriors, 10+ trips/year.
steps.Identify: Consultants, sales reps, executives. Age 28-50. Heavy expense reporting pain.
steps.Report needs: Reliable same-hotel stays, corporate billing, fast check-in, loyalty points consolidation.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest pain: expense reporting and corporate approval workflows.
steps.List solutions: 1) Corporate account with direct billing. 2) Saved preferences (room type, floor, pillow). 3) Loyalty points import from hotel chains. 4) AI itinerary builder.
steps.Evaluate: Corporate billing removes biggest friction. Saved preferences is delight feature. Loyalty import requires partnerships.
steps.Summarize: Corporate billing + saved preferences as MVP. Differentiation vs. hotels.com: personalization at scale.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Identifies corporate billing as key unlock, B2B revenue model insight, loyalty as competitive moat
evaluationRubric.poor: Consumer travel thinking applied to business

questions.question: Design Uber for kids.

sampleAnswer.overview: This is a safety-critical design — I'll structure with CIRCLES and put safety at the center.

steps.Comprehend: Rideshare for minors (under 18), likely 10-17. Parents as payers/approvers.
steps.Identify: Kids: school commute, extracurriculars. Parents: primary decision makers. Drivers: background-checked specialists.
steps.Report needs: Parents: real-time tracking, verified drivers, child check-in. Kids: easy request, safe ride.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Safety and trust are non-negotiables. Can't launch without solving both.
steps.List solutions: 1) Enhanced driver background check + child transport certification. 2) Parent live tracking with ETA. 3) Kid-only confirmation screen with PIN. 4) No cash, parent card only.
steps.Evaluate: Driver certification is highest trust signal. PIN confirmation prevents stranger pickup. Live tracking is table stakes for parents.
steps.Summarize: Launch with certified drivers, parent tracking, PIN confirmation. Trust over growth.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Safety-first framing, parent as decision maker, driver certification insight, PIN/confirmation mechanic
evaluationRubric.fair: Basic safety features, misses driver certification

questions.question: Design a product that helps people learn a new language.

sampleAnswer.overview: Language learning product using CIRCLES.

steps.Comprehend: Mobile app for adult language learners. Assume self-directed, not classroom.
steps.Identify: Casual learners (travel), professional learners (career), heritage speakers reconnecting.
steps.Report needs: Real conversation practice, vocabulary retention, progress feedback, fitting into daily routine.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest failure mode: learners quit after 2 weeks. Key need: habit formation + speaking confidence.
steps.List solutions: 1) AI conversation partner (voice). 2) Spaced repetition for vocabulary. 3) Contextual learning via Netflix subtitles. 4) Streak + social accountability.
steps.Evaluate: AI conversation partner is differentiator. Spaced repetition is proven. Netflix integration is viral but requires licensing.
steps.Summarize: AI voice conversation + spaced repetition as core. Streak mechanic for retention. Skip Netflix for MVP.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Identifies habit formation as core problem, AI conversation as key differentiator, retention mechanics

keyPoints: Habit formation is the real problem

questions.question: You're the PM for Amazon Prime. How would you measure the success of the product?

sampleAnswer.overview: I'll use the DIGS framework: Define goal, Identify metrics, Guard against gaming, Segment.

steps.Define goal: Amazon Prime's goal is to increase customer lifetime value and purchase frequency through loyalty.
steps.Identify metrics: North star: Prime member retention rate (12-month). Supporting: purchase frequency (Prime vs. non-Prime), average order value, streaming hours/month, grocery delivery usage, new Prime signups.
steps.Guard against gaming: Avoid optimizing for sign-ups at cost of retention. Watch for members who sign up for free trial then cancel.
steps.Segment: By tenure (new vs. 2yr+), by usage (streaming heavy vs. shopping heavy), by geography.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Ties metrics to business goal, proposes north star + supporting metrics, guards against gaming, segments
evaluationRubric.good: Multiple metrics with rationale, north star identified
evaluationRubric.poor: One metric or vanity metrics only

keyPoints: Free trial cancellation as gaming risk

questions.question: How would you measure the success of Facebook Stories?

sampleAnswer.overview: Define the goal for Stories, then identify metrics using DIGS.

steps.Define goal: Stories goal: increase daily engagement and shift users toward ephemeral, authentic sharing vs. curated feed posts.
steps.Identify metrics: North star: daily story viewers / DAU. Supporting: stories created per day, story completion rate, reply rate, story-to-feed cannibalization rate.
steps.Guard against gaming: Don't optimize completion rate by making stories shorter — watch content quality. Story creation might cannibalize feed posts.
steps.Segment: Age (Gen Z vs. Millennial), creator vs. viewer, new user vs. power user.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Identifies cannibalization risk, completion rate nuance, creator vs. viewer segmentation

questions.question: You just launched a new podcast discovery feature. What metrics do you track in the first 30 days?

sampleAnswer.overview: New feature launch requires both adoption and quality metrics.

steps.Define goal: Get users to discover and listen to new podcasts they wouldn't have found otherwise.
steps.Identify metrics: Adoption: feature click-through rate. Engagement: podcast plays initiated from discovery. Quality: episode completion rate, saves, subscriptions from discovery. 30-day retention of users who used feature.
steps.Guard against gaming: Don't optimize CTR alone — cheap recommendations inflate clicks. Watch that discovery doesn't just surface popular podcasts (already discoverable).
steps.Segment: New Spotify users vs. existing, podcast-naive vs. existing podcast listeners.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Distinguishes adoption vs. quality, completion rate as quality signal, novelty of recommendations

questions.question: How would you measure the success of Google Maps?

sampleAnswer.overview: Google Maps serves multiple goals — I'll clarify before selecting metrics.

steps.Define goal: Navigation accuracy and usage frequency. Secondary: local business discovery (monetization).
steps.Identify metrics: North star: navigations completed per DAU. Supporting: ETA accuracy (actual vs. predicted time), search-to-route conversion, business listing clicks, offline map usage.
steps.Guard against gaming: ETA accuracy can be gamed by padding estimates. Business click monetization can harm UX if over-optimized.
steps.Segment: Driving vs. transit vs. walking, urban vs. suburban, new user vs. power user.

evaluationRubric.excellent: ETA accuracy as quality metric, business discovery monetization angle, mode of transport segmentation

questions.question: LinkedIn's DAU/MAU ratio dropped 10% last month. How do you investigate?

sampleAnswer.overview: This is a metric drop investigation. I'll diagnose before prescribing.

steps.Define goal: Understand root cause of DAU/MAU drop before taking action.
steps.Identify metrics: Check: is MAU stable or rising (making ratio drop)? Is DAU dropping? Segment by platform (iOS/Android/web), geography, user cohort, feature area.
steps.Guard against gaming: Ensure we're not comparing different definitions of 'active' if any definition changed.
steps.Segment: New vs. returning users, job seekers vs. professionals, mobile vs. desktop.

sampleAnswer.investigationSteps: 1) Confirm data validity — logging bug? 2) Segment by platform. 3) Segment by user type. 4) Check external events (competitor launch, PR issue). 5) Correlate with feature releases.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Checks data validity first, segments systematically, considers external factors, doesn't jump to solution
evaluationRubric.fair: Some segmentation but jumps to solution
evaluationRubric.poor: Immediately suggests a fix without investigation

keyPoints: Don't conflate DAU drop with MAU rise

questions.question: Tell me about a time when you had to make a decision with incomplete information.

sampleAnswer.overview: STAR format: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

steps.Situation: We were launching a new feature to 10% of users. Two days before launch, our analytics showed a potential drop in session length for the test group, but the sample size was only 500 users over 3 days.
steps.Task: Decide whether to delay the launch to get more data or proceed on schedule.
steps.Action: I made a tiered decision: proceed with launch but cap at 5% instead of 10%. Set a clear kill-switch metric (>5% session drop in 48hrs = rollback). Communicated the risk and contingency plan to stakeholders.
steps.Result: Launched successfully. Saw a 2% session drop (within acceptable range). Rolled out to full traffic 2 weeks later after confirming stability.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Specific situation, shows risk framework, quantified threshold, communicated to stakeholders, measured result
evaluationRubric.good: Clear STAR structure, specific decision, outcome stated

questions.question: Describe a situation where you had to influence without authority.

sampleAnswer.overview: STAR for influence without authority.

steps.Situation: Engineering team owned a shared API that was causing latency for my product. They had their own roadmap and my feature wasn't a priority for them.
steps.Task: Get the API performance improvement on their roadmap without direct authority.
steps.Action: I built a business case with user impact data: showed 300ms latency was causing 8% cart abandonment. Aligned with their team's OKR on platform reliability. Proposed a joint sprint with my engineer helping on their backlog in exchange. Got their eng lead to champion it.
steps.Result: Fix was shipped in 6 weeks. Cart abandonment dropped to 3%. Established a cross-team collaboration pattern that became a template.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Data-driven persuasion, OKR alignment tactic, quid-pro-quo offer, systemic outcome

questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed and what you learned.

sampleAnswer.overview: Show genuine self-awareness and learning with STAR.

steps.Situation: I launched a new onboarding flow based on qualitative feedback from 8 user interviews without quantitative validation.
steps.Task: Own the results of the launch.
steps.Action: Shipped to 100% traffic without A/B test because I was confident from user research. New user activation dropped 12% in week one.
steps.Result: Rolled back within 72 hours. I learned to always A/B test even when qualitative data seems conclusive. Now I run every onboarding change through an experiment first. Activation is 6% above original baseline.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Real failure with real numbers, owns it without deflecting, specific learning applied, follow-up improvement

questions.question: Tell me about a product you launched that you're most proud of.

sampleAnswer.overview: Use STAR but focus on impact and PM judgment.

steps.Situation: Led launch of a real-time collaboration feature for a B2B SaaS product. Cross-functional team of 8.
steps.Task: Ship within 4 months to hit enterprise sales cycle.
steps.Action: Ran 3-week discovery sprint with top 5 enterprise customers. Cut scope by 40% to hit deadline. Built in beta with 3 design partners. Ran internal alpha for dogfooding.
steps.Result: Shipped on time. Became #1 reason cited in enterprise deals. Drove 22% expansion revenue in Q3. Went on to expand the feature into an entire product line.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Shows PM craft (discovery, scope decisions, beta), quantified impact, business outcome
evaluationRubric.poor: No PM judgment shown, just shipped a feature

keyPoints: Show PM craft not just shipping

questions.question: Describe a time you disagreed with your manager and how you handled it.

sampleAnswer.overview: Show professional disagreement that's data-driven and respects the relationship.

steps.Situation: Manager wanted to cut user research budget mid-quarter to hit cost targets. I believed the research was critical before a major redesign.
steps.Task: Make the case for keeping research without damaging the relationship.
steps.Action: I didn't push back emotionally. I prepared a risk analysis: what would we not know without research, and what could that cost in rework. Showed 3 examples of past launches that skipped research and needed expensive rework. Proposed a compromise: cut from 20 participants to 8 (still statistically useful).
steps.Result: Manager agreed to the compromise. Ran 8-person study. Found a critical usability issue that would have required 3-week rework. Saved estimated 60 eng-hours.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Data-driven disagreement, preserves relationship, offers compromise, quantified outcome

keyPoints: Show cost of not doing it your way

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to prioritize between multiple competing projects.

sampleAnswer.overview: Show a structured prioritization approach.

steps.Situation: Had 3 high-priority requests land in one week: a critical bug affecting 5% of users, a feature request from our top enterprise client, and an internal tooling improvement requested by engineering.
steps.Task: Decide sequencing with limited sprint capacity.
steps.Action: Applied a modified RICE score to each. Bug: high reach, high impact, high confidence = #1. Enterprise feature: medium reach but strategic revenue risk, direct sales ask = #2. Internal tooling: low urgency, no user impact = deferred to next sprint. Communicated the decision and rationale to each stakeholder proactively.
steps.Result: Bug fixed in 2 days. Enterprise feature shipped following sprint. Engineering team appreciated transparent communication. No stakeholder escalation.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Named framework, stakeholder communication, transparent trade-offs, no escalation
evaluationRubric.good: Clear prioritization logic, multiple stakeholders handled

keyPoints: Bug vs. feature vs. tech debt trade-off

questions.question: Should Apple enter the search engine market?

sampleAnswer.overview: Frame this as a strategic make-vs-buy decision using market analysis.

steps.Strengths: Massive distribution through iOS/Safari. Deep hardware integration. Privacy as differentiator. Strong brand trust.
steps.Weaknesses: No search index. Huge infrastructure investment needed. Late to market. Google relationship at risk (Apple earns ~$18B/year from Google default deal).
steps.Opportunities: AI-native search is a category reset. Privacy-first search has growing demand. Siri could be the interface.
steps.Threats: Google's moat in web crawling and ad revenue. Microsoft/Bing + ChatGPT. User switching costs.
steps.Recommendation: Don't build a traditional search engine — pivot Siri into an AI-first answer engine. Compete on quality of answer, not index size. Start with on-device queries to protect privacy positioning.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Identifies the Google revenue risk, AI-native pivot insight, Siri integration, privacy differentiation

questions.question: Should Google build a smartphone?

sampleAnswer.overview: Strategic entry decision. Google already has Pixel — I'll reframe: should Google double down on hardware vs. remain software-first?

steps.Strengths: AI and ML leadership. Android OS control. Deep data from Google services. Brand trust in tech.
steps.Weaknesses: No manufacturing scale vs. Apple/Samsung. Carrier relationships are weak. Hardware margin is thin.
steps.Opportunities: AI-native phone category. Pixel as Tensor AI showcase. Vertical integration like Apple.
steps.Threats: Apple's ecosystem lock-in. Samsung's scale. Chinese manufacturers on price.
steps.Recommendation: Yes, but stay premium niche. Use Pixel as AI hardware showcase, not volume play. Focus on Tensor chip differentiation.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Reframes question (Pixel exists), AI showcase strategy, niche vs. volume insight

questions.question: Should Amazon enter the healthcare market?

sampleAnswer.overview: Amazon is already in healthcare (Amazon Care, PillPack, One Medical). I'll frame as: how should Amazon expand in healthcare?

steps.Strengths: Logistics and last-mile delivery. AWS for healthcare data. Trust with consumers. Prime relationship.
steps.Weaknesses: No clinical expertise. HIPAA compliance complexity. Physician workforce gap. Regulatory risk.
steps.Opportunities: Pharmacy delivery (PillPack). Primary care (One Medical). Insurance. Wearables + Alexa health.
steps.Threats: CVS/Aetna vertical integration. UnitedHealth scale. Patient trust concerns with data.
steps.Recommendation: Focus on logistics-adjacent: pharmacy delivery and home diagnostics. Avoid direct clinical care where trust and expertise gaps are largest.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Knows Amazon's existing healthcare plays, logistics angle, data trust concern, regulatory
evaluationRubric.poor: Unaware Amazon is already in healthcare

keyPoints: Amazon already has PillPack and One Medical

questions.question: How should Netflix respond to the growth of Disney+?

sampleAnswer.overview: Competitive response strategy for Netflix.

steps.Strengths: Original content library. Global reach. Personalization algorithm. Brand awareness.
steps.Weaknesses: No franchise IP (no Marvel/Star Wars). Content spend is high. Password sharing erodes revenue.
steps.Opportunities: Live events (sports, concerts). Gaming expansion. Ad-supported tier. International originals.
steps.Threats: Disney+, HBO Max, Apple TV+ — fragmentation. Content licensing costs rising. Streaming fatigue.
steps.Recommendation: Double down on global originals (India, Korea, Brazil) where Disney has no local moat. Expand into gaming for engagement. Introduce live events for appointment viewing.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Global originals as moat, gaming expansion insight, live events for appointment viewing, password sharing acknowledgment

keyPoints: No IP library is key weakness

questions.question: What should Microsoft do with its LinkedIn acquisition?

sampleAnswer.overview: LinkedIn + Microsoft integration strategy.

steps.Strengths: LinkedIn's professional network data. Microsoft's enterprise relationships. Office 365 distribution.
steps.Weaknesses: LinkedIn has low daily engagement vs. other social networks. LinkedIn Learning competes with Coursera/Udemy.
steps.Opportunities: LinkedIn data in Microsoft Copilot. Resume import into Teams. CRM integration with Dynamics. Recruiting in Teams workflow.
steps.Threats: Privacy concerns with data integration. User backlash if LinkedIn feels too Microsoft-heavy.
steps.Recommendation: Integrate LinkedIn's professional graph into Microsoft Copilot — hiring, networking, and professional development inside Teams. Keep LinkedIn brand separate to preserve user trust.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Copilot integration insight, professional graph as data asset, brand preservation, CRM angle
evaluationRubric.poor: Just a summary of what LinkedIn does

keyPoints: Professional graph as AI training data

questions.question: You have three features to build but only capacity for one this quarter. How do you prioritize?

sampleAnswer.overview: Use RICE scoring to create objective prioritization.

steps.Reach: Estimate users affected per quarter for each feature.
steps.Impact: Rate 1-3: minimal, significant, massive impact on core metric.
steps.Process: Score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort. Present scores transparently. Discuss assumptions with team. Get stakeholder buy-in on the framework before scoring.

evaluationRubric.excellent: RICE formula articulated, confidence factor noted, stakeholder alignment process, not just math

keyPoints: RICE formula: Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort
Get stakeholder buy-in on framework first

questions.question: Your team's sprint velocity dropped 30%. What do you do?

sampleAnswer.overview: Diagnose before prescribing.

steps.Diagnose: 1) Data: is this one sprint or a trend? 2) Scope creep: did stories grow mid-sprint? 3) Dependencies: blocked on another team? 4) Morale: team events (PTO, attrition)? 5) Tech debt: testing/bugs eating capacity?
steps.Hypotheses: Most common: unplanned work (bugs, incidents), scope creep, or blocking dependencies.
steps.Action: Hold a retrospective focused on blockers. Quantify unplanned work as % of sprint. Negotiate with stakeholders to protect sprint capacity.
steps.Prevention: Add 20% buffer for unplanned work. Define sprint contract: no new items after planning.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Diagnoses before acting, multiple hypotheses, unplanned work quantification, process fix
evaluationRubric.poor: Blames team or adds more process immediately

questions.question: A feature you launched has a bug affecting 5% of users. What do you do?

sampleAnswer.overview: Incident response framework.

steps.Assess severity: 5% of users — how many is that in absolute terms? What's the user impact (data loss vs. UI glitch)? Is it growing?
steps.Immediate actions: If severe: rollback or kill-switch. If minor: hotfix. Notify customer support with FAQ. Update status page if external.
steps.Communicate: Internal: eng lead, support, stakeholders. External: only if user-visible.
steps.Root cause: Post-mortem within 48hrs. 5 Whys. Process fix to prevent recurrence.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Absolute vs. relative framing, rollback consideration, communication plan, post-mortem commitment

questions.question: How do you write a product requirements document (PRD)?

sampleAnswer.overview: PRD structure for a PM interview context.

steps.Problem statement: What user problem are we solving? With evidence.
steps.Goals and non-goals: What success looks like. Explicit non-goals prevent scope creep.
steps.User stories: Who does what and why. Acceptance criteria.
steps.Requirements: Functional (what it does) and non-functional (performance, security, accessibility).
steps.Metrics: How we measure success. Leading and lagging indicators.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Non-goals explicit, acceptance criteria, leading + lagging metrics, open questions

questions.question: Explain how you would design the backend system for a URL shortener.

sampleAnswer.overview: System design for a URL shortener — scope clarification first.

steps.Clarify: Scale: how many URLs/day? Read-heavy or write-heavy? Custom aliases needed? Analytics?
steps.Core components: API (POST /shorten, GET /{code}). Database (URL → code mapping). Cache (Redis for hot URLs). ID generation (base62 encoding of auto-increment ID or hash).
steps.Scale: 100M URLs/day = ~1160 writes/sec. Read-heavy: 10:1 read/write ratio. Use CDN for redirect.
steps.Trade-offs: Hash collision vs. sequential ID. Central ID generator vs. distributed. Cache TTL for popular URLs.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Clarifies scale, cache reasoning, hash vs. sequential trade-off, CDN for performance

questions.question: How does HTTPS work? Why does it matter for a PM?

sampleAnswer.overview: Explain TLS/SSL at a PM-appropriate depth.

steps.How it works: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS. Client and server do a TLS handshake: server presents certificate signed by CA. Both agree on encryption key. All traffic encrypted.
steps.Why PM cares: 1) Trust signal — padlock icon affects conversion rates. 2) SEO — Google ranks HTTPS sites higher. 3) Data privacy — required for PII, payments, HIPAA. 4) Mixed content bugs can break features.
steps.PM implications: Require HTTPS from day one. Audit third-party resources for mixed content. Know that certificate expiry causes outages.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Conversion rate impact, SEO implication, PII/compliance angle, mixed content awareness

questions.question: What is A/B testing and what are common mistakes PMs make with it?

sampleAnswer.overview: A/B testing fundamentals plus pitfalls.

steps.What it is: Randomly assign users to control (A) or variant (B). Measure difference in a target metric. Use statistical significance to decide.
steps.Key concepts: Sample size (determined by minimum detectable effect), statistical significance (p<0.05), test duration (at least 1-2 weeks for seasonality).
steps.Common mistakes: 1) Stopping test early when you see a positive result (peeking problem). 2) Testing too many variants at once. 3) Wrong metric — optimizing for clicks, not conversions. 4) Ignoring segment effects (treatment works for mobile, hurts desktop). 5) No SRM (sample ratio mismatch) check.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Peeking problem, SRM check, segment effects, metric selection issue

questions.question: Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases. When would you use each?

sampleAnswer.overview: SQL vs. NoSQL trade-off for PM context.

steps.SQL: Structured data, fixed schema, ACID transactions. Best for: financial data, relational queries, reporting.
steps.NoSQL: Flexible schema, horizontal scale, eventual consistency. Types: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), columnar (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).
steps.When to use SQL: User account data, orders, inventory — anything requiring strong consistency and joins.
steps.When to use NoSQL: Session data, activity feeds, product catalog with variable attributes, real-time analytics.
steps.PM implication: Schema changes in SQL require migrations (risk). NoSQL is faster to iterate but harder to query.

evaluationRubric.excellent: ACID vs. eventual consistency, migration risk implication, specific NoSQL types, product examples

questions.question: How many gas stations are in the United States?

sampleAnswer.overview: Fermi estimation — show your reasoning, not just the number.

steps.Approach: Bottom-up: how often does a car need gas, and how many cars per station?
steps.Cars in US: 330M people. ~1.5 people per car household. ~220M cars.
steps.Refueling frequency: Car fills up once per week. Station serves customers 14 hours/day. One fill-up takes ~5min. 14×60/5 = 168 fills per pump per day. Typical station has 8 pumps = 1,344 fills/day.
steps.Stations needed: 220M cars / 7 days = 31M fills/day. 31M / 1,344 = ~23,000 stations. (Real answer: ~150,000 — adjust for rural areas, lower utilization.)
steps.Calibration: My estimate of 23K seems low. Add 6x utilization factor for rural/variability = ~140K. Close to real.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Shows reasoning at each step, catches own error, calibrates, close to order of magnitude

keyPoints: Order of magnitude counts, not exact

questions.question: How much revenue does the Google Play Store generate per year?

sampleAnswer.overview: Estimate from top-down: Android users × avg spend.

steps.Android users: ~3B Android devices. ~1B active Google Play users.
steps.Avg spend: Most users spend $0. Active spenders (~20%) spend ~$5/month. 200M × $5 × 12 = $12B gross app revenue.
steps.Real: Google Play was ~$11B in 2021 — my $3B is revenue to Google (not gross). Directionally correct.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Distinguishes gross vs. Google revenue, 30% cut knowledge, active vs. total user distinction
evaluationRubric.fair: Off by more than 10x, some structure

questions.question: How many Amazon Prime members are there?

sampleAnswer.overview: Top-down from US households.

steps.US households: ~130M US households. ~60% own a credit card (prerequisite). ~80M eligible.
steps.Adoption rate: Amazon is dominant e-commerce. ~50% of US households are Prime. 130M × 50% = 65M US Prime.
steps.International: UK, Germany, Japan, India. Total international ~40% of US base = 25M.
steps.Total: ~90M. (Real: ~200M as of 2021 — my estimate is low, India is larger than expected.)
steps.Calibration: India alone has 50M+ Prime subscribers. Adjust upward significantly.

evaluationRubric.excellent: US vs. international split, India as key market, calibrates at end

questions.question: Design a feature to reduce misinformation on Twitter.

sampleAnswer.overview: Content integrity design problem — CIRCLES with trust & safety focus.

steps.Comprehend: Goal: reduce spread of false claims, especially viral ones. Platform: Twitter feed and search.
steps.Identify: Casual readers, news consumers, political activists, bot operators, journalists.
steps.Report needs: Readers: know what's credible. Platform: protect brand and regulators. Journalists: verify sources.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Viral misinformation > fringe misinformation. Focus on high-reach false claims.
steps.List solutions: 1) Friction labels on unverified claims before sharing. 2) Source credibility score. 3) Community Notes (already exists — expand). 4) Slow virality: delay retweets of flagged content.
steps.Evaluate: Friction labels reduce shares but may create Streisand effect. Community Notes is crowd-sourced and scalable. Slow virality is high impact but controversial.
steps.Summarize: Expand Community Notes + friction share labels on automated flagged content. Avoid heavy-handed moderation to preserve free speech perception.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Mentions Community Notes, Streisand effect, virality vs. fringe distinction, regulatory angle

questions.question: Design a social feature for Spotify.

sampleAnswer.overview: Social feature for music streaming — CIRCLES.

steps.Comprehend: Add social layer to Spotify without becoming a social network. Goal: increase session length and retention.
steps.Identify: Casual listeners, music enthusiasts, concert-goers, friends who share music, DJs.
steps.Report needs: Share discoveries with friends, listen together remotely, show off music taste, find concerts.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Listening together (co-listening) and shared discovery have highest retention potential.
steps.List solutions: 1) Jam sessions: sync listening with friends in real time. 2) Taste match: % music compatibility score with friends. 3) Listening activity feed (already existed — was removed). 4) Collaborative playlist with real-time reactions.
steps.Evaluate: Jam sessions is differentiated and drives shared sessions. Taste match is shareable/viral. Activity feed was removed due to privacy complaints — reintroduce with opt-in.
steps.Summarize: Launch Jam sessions + opt-in taste match. Measure: shared session frequency and 30-day retention.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Knows activity feed was removed, opt-in privacy lesson, Jam sessions as retention driver

keyPoints: Activity feed was removed for privacy

questions.question: What metrics would you use to measure the health of Uber's marketplace?

sampleAnswer.overview: Two-sided marketplace metrics — supply and demand must both be healthy.

steps.Define goal: Efficient matching of riders and drivers at acceptable price and wait time.
steps.Identify metrics: Supply: driver utilization rate, driver satisfaction score, driver hours online. Demand: rides completed/day, ride request fulfillment rate, average wait time. Marketplace health: surge pricing frequency, cancellation rate.
steps.Guard against gaming: Optimizing driver utilization alone hurts driver earnings. Wait time SLA can be gamed by surge pricing.
steps.Segment: By city, time of day, ride type (Pool vs. X vs. Black).

evaluationRubric.excellent: Both sides of marketplace, fulfillment rate, surge as health indicator, city segmentation

keyPoints: Two-sided marketplace needs supply AND demand metrics
Surge frequency as marketplace stress signal

questions.question: Tell me about a time you used data to change someone's mind.

sampleAnswer.overview: STAR showing data-driven influence.

steps.Situation: Design team wanted to add a new onboarding modal based on gut feel it would improve activation.
steps.Task: I believed it would hurt activation (added friction) and needed to prove it before building.
steps.Action: Pulled historical data on our previous modal experiment. Showed it caused 15% drop in day-1 retention for new users. Ran a quick survey with 50 new users — 70% said they'd skip the modal. Presented findings in design review.
steps.Result: Team agreed to test the modal with 10% traffic first. Test confirmed: 12% drop in activation. Modal was redesigned with skip option and deployed to full traffic with 4% activation improvement.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Historical data + user research combo, proposed test instead of kill, outcome measured
evaluationRubric.good: Clear data use, changed mind, measured

questions.question: What should Google do with YouTube in the next 5 years?

sampleAnswer.overview: YouTube 5-year strategic vision.

steps.Strengths: 2B+ MAU. Creator ecosystem. Ad revenue leader. Live streaming. Shorts growing.
steps.Weaknesses: Advertiser-hostile content (brand safety). Creator burnout and revenue complaints. No subscription killer app.
steps.Opportunities: Podcasts (moving from audio). Shopping integration (YouTube → buy). AI content tools for creators. Gaming/esports.
steps.Threats: TikTok taking short-form attention. Twitch for gaming. Spotify for podcasts. Regulatory scrutiny.
steps.Recommendation: Double down on Shorts + shopping integration (YouTube → commerce). Build AI creator tools to reduce production cost barrier. Expand podcast hosting to compete with Spotify.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Commerce integration, AI creator tools, podcast threat from Spotify, Shorts vs. TikTok competition

questions.question: How do you manage a product roadmap with 10 stakeholders, all of whom have different priorities?

sampleAnswer.overview: Roadmap alignment with many stakeholders.

steps.Framework: 1) Align on company OKRs first — everything flows from there. 2) Map each stakeholder request to an OKR. 3) RICE score requests. 4) Time-box stakeholder input sessions.
steps.Process: Quarterly roadmap review: 1-hour sessions with each stakeholder. Present RICE scores. Have them challenge assumptions, not override scores.
steps.Conflict resolution: When two OKRs conflict, escalate to leadership for prioritization. Don't resolve strategic conflicts at PM level.
steps.Communication: Publish roadmap with rationale. 'No' with reasoning is better than silence. Regular 30-day updates.

evaluationRubric.excellent: OKR-first alignment, escalation protocol, 'no with reasoning', published rationale

keyPoints: Map requests to OKRs before scoring

questions.question: Design Google's next hardware product.

sampleAnswer.overview: Google hardware strategy — what gap exists in the ecosystem?

steps.Comprehend: What problem space? Google's hardware strengths: AI/ML, ambient computing, home automation.
steps.Identify: Smart home users, health-conscious consumers, remote workers, seniors.
steps.Report needs: Ambient health monitoring, smart home integration, AI accessibility for non-tech users.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Biggest unserved: health monitoring without wearable fatigue.
steps.List solutions: 1) Smart mirror with health analytics. 2) AI-powered hearing aid. 3) Ambient health sensor (non-wearable). 4) Smart glasses 2.0 with AI overlay.
steps.Evaluate: Smart glasses: AR opportunity but Google Glass failed on privacy. Ambient health sensor: no privacy issue, passive, meaningful data. Hearing aid: underserved segment with assistive + AI tie-in.
steps.Summarize: AI hearing aid — addresses accessibility, assistive tech market, AI assistant integration, premium price point.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Google Glass failure lesson, ambient vs. wearable distinction, accessibility angle, AI integration

keyPoints: AI hearing aid as novel suggestion

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a stakeholder.

sampleAnswer.overview: STAR for delivering bad news.

steps.Situation: We had to delay a major feature launch by 6 weeks due to a security vulnerability found in code review.
steps.Task: Tell the VP of Sales who had committed the feature to enterprise customers.
steps.Action: Met in person (not email). Led with the reason and the plan, not the apology. Gave specific new date with confidence level. Offered to join sales calls to explain to affected customers. Came with two mitigation options (partial feature vs. delay).
steps.Result: VP appreciated the directness and plan. Chose partial feature release. One enterprise customer accepted, one asked for contract extension. No revenue lost.

evaluationRubric.excellent: In person delivery, led with plan not apology, offered mitigation options, quantified outcome
evaluationRubric.poor: Delayed telling, or told via email

keyPoints: Deliver in person not via email

questions.question: How would you measure trust on the Airbnb platform?

sampleAnswer.overview: Trust is a latent metric — you have to measure it through proxies.

steps.Define goal: Trust = hosts trust guests, guests trust hosts, both trust Airbnb as a platform.
steps.Identify metrics: Guest side: booking conversion rate, review submission rate, repeat bookings. Host side: acceptance rate, superhost retention, listing accuracy complaints. Platform: dispute rate, ID verification completion, response time to issues.
steps.Guard against gaming: High review rates can be coerced. Dispute rate can be suppressed by settling quickly without fixing root cause.
steps.Segment: New host vs. experienced host. New guest vs. returning. Domestic vs. international. Long-stay vs. short-stay.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Both sides of marketplace, coercion risk in reviews, dispute suppression risk, segmentation

questions.question: Design a product to improve the college application process.

sampleAnswer.overview: High-stakes design problem with multiple user types.

steps.Comprehend: Scope: application process for US colleges, 17-18 year olds.
steps.Identify: Students, parents, high school counselors, college admissions officers.
steps.Report needs: Students: organize applications, understand fit, reduce anxiety. Counselors: track students. Admissions: read apps efficiently.
steps.Cut/Prioritize: Students are primary users. Biggest pain: organization across 10+ schools, essay reuse, deadline tracking.
steps.List solutions: 1) Dashboard: all applications, deadlines, status. 2) Essay builder with reuse across applications. 3) Fit score: student vs. school profile match. 4) College counselor portal.
steps.Evaluate: Dashboard + essay builder solve immediate pain. Fit score is differentiated but requires data partnerships. Counselor portal opens B2B revenue.
steps.Summarize: Launch with student dashboard + essay builder. Add counselor portal in phase 2 for institutional revenue.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Multi-user design, essay reuse insight, counselor as B2B opportunity, fit score data challenge

questions.question: How should Apple respond to ChatGPT and the rise of generative AI?

sampleAnswer.overview: Apple's AI strategy in the generative AI era.

steps.Strengths: On-device processing (privacy). A-series and M-series chips. Apple Silicon neural engine. Consumer trust. Siri installed base.
steps.Weaknesses: Siri is behind GPT-4 and Gemini. No cloud AI infrastructure like Azure/GCP. Slow to open AI to developers.
steps.Opportunities: On-device AI = private AI (regulatory tailwind). Apple Intelligence as a brand. AI in every app via APIs. Healthcare AI (Apple Watch data).
steps.Threats: Google Gemini on Android. Microsoft Copilot in enterprise. OpenAI partnerships with Samsung.
steps.Recommendation: Double down on on-device private AI as differentiator. Ship Apple Intelligence across all apps. Open to developers via a privacy-safe API. Don't compete on model size — compete on privacy and integration.

evaluationRubric.excellent: On-device privacy angle, Apple Intelligence awareness, developer API, not competing on model size

questions.question: How would you improve Meta AI, Meta's AI assistant?

sampleAnswer.overview: Start by clarifying what Meta AI currently does (the AI layer), then segment users, identify the highest-pain problem for your chosen segment, propose 3+ solutions, prioritize with explicit criteria including safety, and define success metrics using SIGNAL.
steps: Clarify: Meta AI is a general-purpose LLM assistant integrated across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger — it answers questions, generates content, and helps with tasks.
User segments: (1) casual social users who stumble on it, (2) small business owners using it for content creation, (3) creators building audiences, (4) users seeking information instead of search.
Pick small business owners — highest commercial intent, clearest ROI measurement, biggest gap between what they need and what generic LLMs provide.
Problems: (1) AI-generated posts sound generic and don't match their brand voice, (2) can't incorporate their actual business data (inventory, pricing, hours), (3) no continuity between sessions.
Solutions: (a) brand voice training from their existing posts, (b) business profile integration for inventory/pricing context, (c) persistent memory of their business.
Recommend: brand voice feature — highest value, feasible with RAG on their post history, no privacy risk since it's their own content.
AI failure path: generated post sounds off-brand. Show 'trained on your last 50 posts' with a 1-tap regenerate. Log user edits to improve the model.
Metrics (C-NABGT): North Star = posts generated and published without editing. Guardrail = user override rate must stay below 30%.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Clarifies the AI layer first, picks ONE user segment and justifies it, names why AI is better than non-AI for this problem, proposes an AI failure path without being asked, uses C-NABGT or SIGNAL for metrics.
evaluationRubric.good: Has clear user segmentation and picks one, proposes reasonable solutions, mentions metrics — but skips failure path or doesn't justify why AI specifically.
evaluationRubric.fair: Identifies users and problems but designs for multiple segments, or proposes a single solution without tradeoffs, or metrics are vague ('engagement').
evaluationRubric.poor: Jumps to features without users or problem, no metrics, no consideration of AI failure modes.

keyPoints: Must clarify what the AI layer does before designing improvements
AI failure path is required — what does the UI show when the AI generates bad content?
North Star metric must be a count, not a ratio
User override rate is the honesty metric for AI trust

questions.source: CrackPMInterview Complete AI PM Interview Guide 2026
questions.question: Design an AI tool for small business owners who want to manage their customer relationships.

sampleAnswer.overview: Apply the 10-step design framework. The key differentiator from a standard CRM: the AI layer must handle probabilistic outputs (AI might misremember a customer), and the onboarding path is critical because small business owners are skeptical of AI accuracy.
steps: Clarifying Questions: Mobile or desktop? US-focused? B2C or B2B small businesses? (Assume mobile-first, B2C, US, <10 employees.)

User Segments: (1) solo freelancers tracking clients, (2) restaurant owners with regulars, (3) retail shop owners with repeat customers, (4) service providers (plumbers, cleaners). Pick restaurant owners — high repeat purchase frequency, clear ROI for remembering preferences.
Problem: Owner can't remember which customers are regulars, their preferences, or when they last visited — relies on memory or expensive POS software.

Solution options: (a) AI that scans receipts and builds customer profiles automatically, (b) voice note to customer profile ('Sarah likes window table, no onions'), (c) AI suggests personalized follow-up messages.
Recommend voice note to profile — lowest friction for busy owners, no receipt scanning setup, clear AI value (transcription + structuring).

Core flows: Happy path: owner taps mic, says 'Mark always orders the salmon', AI transcribes and adds to Mark's profile. AI failure path: AI mishears 'salmon' as 'salami' — show transcription for quick correction before saving. Onboarding path: first-time user sees 3 example profiles pre-populated, with an explanation of how AI learned them.

Safety/risks: Customer data privacy — what happens if the device is lost? Mitigation: profiles encrypted, no PII visible on lock screen. Risk at scale: AI suggestions become generic as customer base grows — need refresh logic.
Metrics: North Star = customer profiles with at least one AI-generated note that the owner kept (didn't delete). Guardrail = transcription error rate below 5%.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Follows all 10 steps, explicitly designs the AI failure path AND the onboarding path, raises privacy risk proactively, ends with a compelling narrative and metrics.
evaluationRubric.good: Strong user segmentation and solution design, mentions risks when asked, but only covers the happy path in core flows.
evaluationRubric.fair: Reasonable problem statement and solution, but skips core flows entirely or gives only happy path, no metrics.
evaluationRubric.poor: Jumps to features without users or problem, no flows, no metrics, no safety consideration.

keyPoints: AI failure path and onboarding path are as important as the happy path
Safety must be raised proactively — not when prompted
Compelling narrative: owner should be able to repeat the product in one sentence
The AI layer must be justified — why voice note to profile vs. just a notes app?

questions.question: Your AI feature's user override rate has been rising for 3 weeks. Walk me through how you'd investigate.

sampleAnswer.overview: This is a metric drop question (use TROPIC + AI layer) disguised as a product question. User override rate rising means users are increasingly rejecting AI outputs — it's a trust signal, not just an accuracy metric.
steps: Rule out data bugs first: is the override rate tracking correctly? Did we change the definition of 'override' recently?
T (Time): Sudden or gradual over the 3 weeks? A sudden jump points to a specific cause (model update, feature change). Gradual points to drift.
R (Region): All users, or specific geographies? Suggests localization issues.
O (Other launches): Did we change the prompt, update the model, or ship a UI change around the start of the trend?
P (Platform): iOS vs Android vs desktop? Suggests rendering or latency issues.
I (Industry): Are competitors' AI products showing similar user frustration signals? Suggests external cause.
C (Cannibalization): Did we add another AI feature that handles the same use case better?
AI layer (most likely cause): Silent model update or prompt change degraded output quality. Check: did hallucination rate rise at the same time? Did task completion rate fall?
Hypothesis: Model update changed output style — users expected X, got Y. Run A/B test comparing old vs. new model behavior on the same input set.
Recommendation: If model update is confirmed, roll back to previous version while diagnosing. Add override reason logging so future drops are diagnosable faster.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Uses TROPIC explicitly, adds the AI-specific layer without prompting, distinguishes diagnosis from prescription, makes a clear rollback recommendation with conditions.
evaluationRubric.good: Systematically investigates causes, mentions model updates, makes a recommendation — but doesn't use TROPIC structure or conflates diagnosis with prescription.
evaluationRubric.fair: Lists some investigation steps but jumps to a fix early, misses the AI-specific layer (model update, hallucination rate).
evaluationRubric.poor: Treats rising override rate as a UI problem without investigating AI layer, no structured diagnostic process.

keyPoints: User override rate = trust signal, not just accuracy metric
TROPIC applies to any metric drop including AI-specific ones
Always add the AI layer: model update? drift? hallucination rate change?
Rule out data bugs before assuming a product problem

questions.question: How do you approach safety in a consumer AI product?

sampleAnswer.overview: Use P-PRIME: start with product context, enumerate the specific risk categories that apply, design mitigations, implement guardrails, monitor, and iterate. Safety must be designed in from the start — not added as a final checklist.
steps: P (Product context): What is the product, who are the users, what scale? A coding assistant for developers has different risk profile than a health information chatbot for general consumers.

P (Potential risks): (1) Harmful content generation (self-harm instructions, dangerous how-tos), (2) Bias in outputs affecting specific groups differently, (3) Data privacy (model trained on user data, PII leakage), (4) Adversarial misuse (jailbreaks, prompt injection).
R (Risk mitigation): Content classifiers on output before display, confidence thresholds that trigger human review for high-stakes queries, opt-in rather than opt-out for sensitive contexts.
I (Implementation guardrails): Rate limiting to limit abuse at scale, structured output formats that constrain model freedom, clear disclosure that outputs are AI-generated.
M (Monitoring and metrics): Harmful output rate (human rated sample weekly), abuse report rate per 1K users, bias metrics across demographic segments.
E (Evolution): Red-team testing quarterly, user feedback loops for reporting harmful outputs, model version rollback capability when safety regressions detected.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Names all four risk categories, designs safety into the product flow (not as an afterthought), defines specific monitoring metrics with measurement cadence.
evaluationRubric.good: Covers most risk categories, proposes reasonable mitigations, mentions monitoring — but monitoring is vague ('we'd track harmful outputs' without specifics).
evaluationRubric.fair: Mentions 1-2 risk categories, proposes content filtering as the only mitigation, no monitoring plan.
evaluationRubric.poor: Treats safety as a single concern ('just add a content filter'), no risk enumeration, no monitoring.

keyPoints: Four risk categories: harmful content, bias, privacy, adversarial misuse
Safety designed in from step 1 — not a final checklist
Monitoring plan must specify measurement method AND cadence
Red-team testing is a product responsibility, not just an ML team responsibility

questions.source: CrackPMInterview Complete AI PM Interview Guide 2026
questions.question: Your AI gave harmful advice to a vulnerable user. Walk me through your incident response.

sampleAnswer.overview: This is an operational decision question. The structure: contain immediately, investigate root cause, communicate transparently, fix and verify, build prevention into the system.
steps: Immediate containment: Disable or limit the specific capability that caused the harm if it can be isolated. Log the full conversation for investigation. Do not delete — it's evidence.
User triage: Does the affected user need immediate support resources? If the harm is ongoing (e.g., self-harm advice), surface crisis resources immediately.
Root cause: Was this a model failure (hallucination, misaligned output), a prompt injection attack, or a gap in content classifiers? Reproduce the failure in a sandbox.

Communication: Notify legal and trust & safety within 1 hour. If reportable under applicable regulations (GDPR, state AI laws), begin that process. Communicate honestly with the affected user if possible.
Fix: Update content classifiers for this category. Add this case to the red-team test suite. Tighten system prompt guardrails. If root cause is model-level, escalate to ML team with evidence.
Prevention: Add this failure mode to the formal safety monitoring dashboard. Run a broader audit: how many similar conversations exist in logs?

evaluationRubric.excellent: Leads with user safety (not company protection), distinguishes model failure from prompt injection, includes regulatory communication step, adds the case to ongoing monitoring.
evaluationRubric.good: Has a reasonable incident response structure, mentions root cause investigation and fix — but misses user welfare step or regulatory communication.
evaluationRubric.fair: Focuses on technical fix only, skips affected user welfare, no prevention or monitoring.
evaluationRubric.poor: Treats as a PR problem, no root cause investigation, no monitoring update.

keyPoints: Lead with user safety — not company liability protection
Distinguish model failure from prompt injection: different root causes, different fixes
Add the case to red-team suite immediately — this is a prevention action
Regulatory reporting is a product responsibility PM must know about

questions.question: How would you prevent harmful outputs from a deployed chatbot at scale?

sampleAnswer.overview: Prevention is a layered system, not a single control. The layers: pre-deployment (red-team, eval suite), deployment (classifiers, rate limits, structured outputs), monitoring (sampling + automated evals), and iteration (feedback loops).
steps: Pre-deployment: Red-team testing with adversarial prompts targeting each risk category. Define an eval suite: what harmful output rate is acceptable before launch? (e.g., <0.1% on a standardized test set.)
Input layer: Classify user inputs for intent before sending to the model. High-risk intent queries go to restricted response templates or human review queue.
Output layer: Classifier on model outputs before display. Flag outputs above harm threshold. Uncertain cases trigger safe fallback response + option to speak with human.
Structural controls: System prompt guardrails, structured output format that constrains model freedom, refusal templates for specific harm categories.
Scale controls: Rate limiting to limit how much any single user can extract, anomaly detection for prompt injection patterns.
Monitoring: Weekly human-rated sample (1% of flagged outputs), automated eval suite run on every model update, bias metrics across demographic groups.
Iteration: Public disclosure policy for safety incidents, red-team quarterly updates as attack vectors evolve.

evaluationRubric.excellent: Covers all three prevention layers (pre-deployment, deployment, monitoring), names specific metrics with thresholds, mentions bias monitoring across groups.
evaluationRubric.good: Has input and output classifiers, mentions monitoring — but monitoring is vague, no pre-deployment red-team, no bias consideration.
evaluationRubric.fair: Mentions a content filter as the main control, some monitoring — but single-layer prevention.
evaluationRubric.poor: Content filter only, no monitoring plan, no pre-deployment testing.

keyPoints: Prevention is layered: pre-deployment + deployment + monitoring + iteration
Define acceptable harm rate threshold BEFORE launch
Bias monitoring is part of safety monitoring, not a separate concern
Rate limiting is a safety control, not just a cost control

questions.question: How would you measure the success of ChatGPT as a product?

sampleAnswer.overview: Use C-NABGT. The key insight: accuracy metrics alone are insufficient for an AI product — you need user behavior signals that reveal actual trust and value delivery.
steps: C (Clarify): ChatGPT for consumers, not API users. Time window: 6-month lagging indicators + leading weekly metrics.
N (North Star): Weekly active users who complete at least one multi-turn conversation (not just a single query) — this measures habitual value delivery, not one-time curiosity.

A (Actionable secondary metrics): (1) Task completion rate (user got what they came for — measured by session ending without re-query on same topic), (2) User override rate (user corrected or dismissed output — the honesty metric for AI trust), (3) Conversation depth (average turns per session — proxy for value delivered).
B (Business metrics): DAU/MAU ratio (stickiness), revenue per user, churn rate by user segment.
G (Guardrails): Harmful output rate must stay below 0.1% (human-rated sample). Hallucination rate on factual queries below 5%. TTFT (time to first token) below 500ms p95.

T (Tracking plan): Task completion rate = session ends without follow-up query on same topic within 10 minutes (automated). User override rate = explicit edit/copy-without-edit behavior (instrumented in UI). Harmful output rate = weekly human-rated random sample of 1,000 flagged conversations.

evaluationRubric.excellent: North Star is an absolute count (not ratio), includes user override rate as AI-specific trust metric, defines tracking plan with specific measurement method for each metric, guardrails include AI-specific thresholds (hallucination rate, TTFT).
evaluationRubric.good: Reasonable North Star and secondary metrics, mentions AI-specific metrics — but tracking plan is vague ('we'd instrument the UI'), or guardrails are generic.
evaluationRubric.fair: DAU or revenue as North Star (not wrong but not differentiated for an AI product), secondary metrics are generic engagement metrics, no AI-specific guardrails.
evaluationRubric.poor: Vague metrics like 'engagement' or 'satisfaction' with no definition of how to measure them, no tracking plan.

keyPoints: North Star must be an absolute count, not an average or ratio
User override rate is the AI trust signal — always include it
The T (Tracking plan) in C-NABGT separates strong from weak answers
AI guardrails: hallucination rate + TTFT are product metrics, not just ML metrics

questions.question: Snap is deploying an LLM-powered feature. What metrics would you track to evaluate its performance?

sampleAnswer.overview: Use SIGNAL. Snap's context matters: a young, mobile-first user base with low tolerance for latency and high sensitivity to privacy. The metrics must reflect the probabilistic nature of LLM outputs AND Snap's specific product context.
steps: S (Scope): LLM feature within Snap's messaging/stories context. Users: 13-25 primarily. Time window: first 90 days post-launch for leading indicators.
I (Identify goal): Users adopt the AI feature into their regular Snap usage — it becomes a habitual part of how they communicate or discover content.

G (Generate candidate metrics): Task completion rate, re-query rate (user rephrased and tried again = AI failed), latency (TTFT for mobile), override rate, feature retention at D7/D30, content quality reports.
N (Negative guardrails): Re-query rate must stay below 25% (high re-query = AI not understanding intent). TTFT must stay below 800ms on mobile 4G. Content policy violation rate below 0.05%.

A (Anchor on North Star): D7 feature retention — percentage of users who used the feature in week 1 and returned in week 2. This is more honest than DAU because it measures habitual value, not just novelty.
L (Layer breakdowns): By platform (iOS vs Android — latency differs), by age segment (13-17 vs 18-25 — usage patterns differ), by query type (informational vs. creative vs. social).

evaluationRubric.excellent: Uses SIGNAL explicitly, anchors North Star on retention (not novelty), includes Snap-specific context (mobile, young users, latency sensitivity), defines guardrail thresholds, includes L (breakdowns).
evaluationRubric.good: Reasonable metrics with AI-specific considerations, mentions retention — but guardrails are generic or missing thresholds, no breakdowns.
evaluationRubric.fair: DAU or activation rate as North Star without retention signal, some AI metrics — but no context-awareness of Snap's constraints.
evaluationRubric.poor: Generic app metrics (downloads, DAU), no AI-specific metrics, no guardrails.

keyPoints: North Star should be retention-based, not activation-based (novelty does not equal value)
Mobile latency is a guardrail, not just an engineering concern
SIGNAL's L (breakdowns) is what makes the analysis actionable
Re-query rate = intent understanding failure — more honest than accuracy

questions.question: The hallucination rate for your AI feature doubled after last week's model update. What do you do?

sampleAnswer.overview: This is a metric drop question — use TROPIC + AI layer. A doubled hallucination rate after a model update is almost certainly caused by the model update, but you still need to follow the diagnostic process to be sure.
steps: T (Time): Was the doubling sudden on the day of the model update, or gradual since? Sudden = model update is the cause. Gradual = other factors.
R (Region): All users or specific geographies/languages? If only in non-English markets, the new model may have worse multilingual performance.
O (Other launches): Did we also change the prompt, the retrieval system (if RAG), or any UI that affects what users query at the same time as the model update?
P (Platform): iOS vs Android vs desktop? If hallucination rate is higher on mobile, it could be a context window truncation issue.
I (Industry): Are other products using the same model reporting similar issues? Check the model provider's status page and developer forums.
C (Cannibalization): Not applicable here.

AI Layer: Most likely cause — the new model version has lower factual accuracy on our specific use case. Confirm: (1) Run our eval suite on old vs. new model, (2) Check if the model provider's release notes mention accuracy tradeoffs.

Recommendation: If eval suite confirms regression, roll back to previous model version immediately. File a report with the model provider. Run the eval suite on every future model update before deploying to production (add this as a deployment gate).

evaluationRubric.excellent: Uses TROPIC explicitly, adds the AI-specific layer without prompting, recommends rollback with clear condition, adds eval suite as a permanent deployment gate.
evaluationRubric.good: Systematically investigates, checks model update as primary cause, recommends rollback — but doesn't use TROPIC structure, or doesn't add eval suite as future prevention.
evaluationRubric.fair: Identifies model update as likely cause, recommends rollback — but no systematic investigation, no prevention step.
evaluationRubric.poor: Assumes it's a model problem without investigation, recommends asking engineers to 'fix the model' without a structured response.

keyPoints: TROPIC applies to AI-specific metric drops too
Model update is the first AI-layer hypothesis — confirm with eval suite, don't assume
Rollback is a valid product decision — have the capability ready
Eval suite before deployment is the prevention lesson from this incident
